Founder and President/Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, has disclosed that his company paid interest rates of up to 40 per cent to local banks while financing the construction of its Obajana Cement plant in Kogi State. Dangote said the project, initially estimated to cost 1bn, faced delays due to infrastructure deficiencies and other operational challenges. He stated this on Thursday at the 25th annual conference of Women in Management and Business in Lagos, where he encouraged women entrepreneurs to venture into industrial businesses and pursue ambitious investment plans. Recounting the financial difficulties involved in developing the Obajana plant, which is now Dangote Cement’s flagship facility, he said the company borrowed from local banks when its capital stood at N25bn. “You won’t believe how much interest we were paying when we built Obajana (Kogi State, Nigeria). I tell you, we were able to do it when the banks were at N25bn capital. And we took on a project of $`180m,” Dangote said. He explained that the company did not initially invest in essential infrastructure such as gas pipelines, fuel facilities and power plants because it expected the government to provide adequate public utilities. “So we ended up having a problem. We didn’t put in a gas pipeline, we didn’t put fuel in, we didn’t put in a power plant. All these things, because the government announced that we’d be having enough power, we’d be having enough this and that,” he said. The infrastructure shortfalls, he added, contributed to the increase in the project’s cost to $1bn, prompting the company to seek additional financing from the International Finance Corporation. According to Dangote, the IFC rejected the company’s proposed three-year repayment plan after assessing its financial projections and instead offered a longer repayment arrangement. “We wanted to pay within three years, but when the IFC used their own financial model, they said our business plan was wrong. They gave us seven years. They said in the first two years we cannot pay anything. Then, in five years, is the payment period,” he said. Despite the extended repayment arrangement, Dangote said borrowing from Nigerian banks remained expensive, with interest rates reaching 40 per cent. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. But we were paying interest at 40 per cent to the local banks. They can check the records,” he said. He said he eventually invited the bankers to dinner six months before the expiration of the 18-month financing arrangement and settled the outstanding loans. “On the 18th month, six months before the expiry, I invited the bankers to dinner, and at the end of the dinner, I gave everybody their cheque. I paid off,” he said. Obajana is Dangote Cement’s largest Nigerian factory, with an installed capacity of 16.25 million tonnes per annum across five production lines. The plant was commissioned in 2007 with two lines and a combined capacity of five million tonnes per annum. Its capacity was increased to 10.25 million tonnes per annum in 2012 following the addition of a third line. Two further production lines, each with a capacity of three million tonnes per annum, were added in late 2014 and 2020. Dangote also recounted the difficulties encountered in developing the Dangote Petroleum Refinery, saying international engineering companies and other industry players initially doubted the feasibility of the project. He said the company first planned to build a refinery with a capacity of 300,000 barrels per day but later increased the target to 650,000 barrels per day, despite warnings about the scale of the undertaking. According to him, some international engineering, procurement and construction contractors declined to work on the project because they considered Nigeria too risky. He said the company eventually took on the role of its own EPC contractor and completed a refinery whose capacity has since exceeded its initial design. “We’re able not only to deliver the 650,000, which they say will not be done. We now are at 710,000 barrels,” he said. The industrialist urged women entrepreneurs to be ambitious, set clear targets and take calculated risks in pursuing their business goals. “Don’t let anybody tell you that you are not able to do it. You must think very, very big. You must be very ambitious. You must give yourself a target and believe that you can deliver that target,” he said. He also identified inadequate infrastructure as a major challenge facing businesses in Nigeria, noting that some companies had to invest in facilities that should ordinarily be provided through public infrastructure. “We are facing a lot of issues in terms of infrastructure. And right now, sometimes, what we do is we put the money down. I would like to build this infrastructure, and then we just do it on our own,” he said. Dangote further urged business leaders to remain resilient in the face of setbacks, saying entrepreneurship and industrial investments often come with significant challenges. “There is nothing in life that is easy. So you must say that yes, it’s difficult for me, but I can surmount all these pressures,” he said. He also said the Dangote Petroleum Refinery was expected to record the highest profitability on the African continent within 55 days, describing profitability as the company’s immediate priority. Earlier, the Founding Chairperson and Trustee of WIMBIZ, Omobola Johnson, reflected on the organisation’s 25-year history and its efforts to build a lasting platform for women in business and management. Johnson said the founders had sustained their commitment through inclusion, mutual respect, shared leadership and effective succession planning. She said WIMBIZ had also challenged the notion that women could not work together, citing the organisation’s continued growth over the years. “We countered the fallacy that women cannot work together. We have worked together for 25 years, and we have built an institution that has endured, stood the test of time,” Johnson said. She added that the founders had placed their collective vision above personal interests and ethnic differences while promoting diversity and a shared purpose.
